About

Hardware that thinks.

I design machines from the structure up, then give them senses and intelligence. Mechanical engineering is the foundation. Automation and AI are what make it adapt.

  1. 01

    Mechanical design is the body

    Strong, light and manufacturable. If the structure is wrong, no amount of software can fix it.

  2. 02

    Sensors are the senses

    A machine that cannot measure itself cannot improve itself. Good data starts with good hardware.

  3. 03

    Control and AI are the brain

    Control, learning and optimization turn a machine into a system that adapts and keeps getting better.

  4. 04

    Automation removes the repetition

    Anything an engineer does a thousand times should be a macro, so the time goes into design decisions.

  5. 05

    My mission

    Driving mechanical design towards AI-powered and intelligent systems: machines built to sense, decide and improve.

        MaterialsExperiment

        Rolling temperature and the strength of an aluminum composite

        Bachelor's thesis, B.Tech Mechanical Engineering, VIT Vellore, April 2023. With Harssha A. Guide: Dr. P. Seenuvasaperumal.

        Aluminum 2014 is light and strong, but its strength is not enough for demanding structural uses. The thesis cast Al2014 with in-situ ZrB₂ reinforcement and compared how rolling at cryogenic, room and warm temperatures changes its hardness, strength and ductility.

        My part: literature review on in-situ ZrB₂ fabrication, the casting process, the rolling process, hardness and tensile tests, and documentation.

        Compare the four rolling conditions

        Values from Table 3.1 of the thesis. CR is cryo rolling, RTR room-temperature rolling, HR hot (warm) rolling; all reach 40% total reduction.

        Process

        • Squeeze casting at 800 °C pouring, 400 °C mould, 100 MPa pressure
        • In-situ ZrB₂ formed from K₂ZrF₆ and KBF₄ salts, 5 wt% in the composite
        • Samples cut by wire-cut EDM, 15 in total
        • Homogenized at 504 °C for 2 hours, then water quenched

        Findings

        • Cryo rolling gave the highest hardness: 188 HV for CR40%
        • CR20%+RTR20% reached the highest yield strength, 270 MPa
        • Cryogenic temperatures limit dislocation movement and suppress dynamic recovery
        • 40% reduction elongates and breaks grains but does not fully refine them

        Characterization

        • Hardness and tensile testing
        • Optical microscopy at 5x and 20x
        • XRD on a Bruker D8-QUEST
        • Literature gap: few studies on ZrB₂ in-situ Al2014 composites

        Tools: squeeze casting furnace, wire-cut EDM, muffle furnace, 2-high rolling mill, hardness and tensile testers, optical microscope, XRD

        HardwareSimulation

        Energy-efficient heated bed for FDM 3D printing

        Interdisciplinary Engineering Project, TU Clausthal, 10/2024 – 03/2025. Group B7 with Nikhil Vinayagamurthy, Ashwanth Kumar C R and Hithesh Alen D Costa.

        University lab printers suffer from warping, poor bed adhesion and wasted energy. The team designed a modular heated bed that heats only the zones a print needs, simulated it in ANSYS Workbench, then built and tested a prototype.

        Thermistor to temperature

        The same Beta equation as the Arduino sketch: B = 3950, R₀ = 100 kΩ at 25 °C.

        °C

        Near the 70 °C operating point the thermistor reads about 17.6 kΩ.

        Built

        • Borosilicate glass print surface
        • Aluminum-foil resistive heating elements in modular zones
        • Insulation layer to cut heat loss
        • Arduino with MOSFET switching
        • 5 NTC thermistors on analog pins A2 to A6

        Results

        • Stable bed temperature of about 70 °C
        • Reached in roughly 8 minutes
        • Suitable for PETG and TPU
        • Two heating modes avoid heating unused area
        • Thermistor cutoff for overheating protection

        Source material

        • GitHub repository
        • Circuit schematic (PDF)
        • Arduino sketch
        • Video: ANSYS workflow
        • Video: center-bed simulation
        • Video: full-bed simulation

        Tools: ANSYS Workbench, Arduino IDE, MOSFET switching circuits, thermistors, FDM printing

        DesignThermal

        Rover that carries medicine at a regulated temperature

        Lab Design for Industry 4.0, TU Clausthal, group D-5 with Sai Akash Kumar S. V. K., Sabin Cristanious Samraj and Nithin Gengamuthu. Guided by Prof. Dr.-Ing. David Inkermann.

        Temperature-sensitive medicine must stay at 10 °C ± 1 °C on the way to the patient. The group designed an upgraded rover with a Peltier-cooled, insulated compartment for a 40 × 20 × 80 mm container, plus tracking, monitoring and a backup power source.

        Insulation thickness

        d = A · ΔT · k / Q, the formula from the report. Defaults are the report's assumptions: 25 °C ambient, k = 0.03 W/(m·K), A = 1 m², Q = 10 W.

        cm

        Requirements

        • 10 ± 1 °C inside the container
        • 3 kg of extra load without further modification
        • Real-time position and temperature tracking
        • Backup power for cooling and position reports
        • Bolted, screw and snap joints for easy maintenance

        Design

        • Peltier module with cold side about −8 °C and hot side about +70 °C
        • 50 mm Styrofoam, matching the 4.5 cm calculation
        • Estimated added weight of 1200 to 1800 g
        • Wheel change from 120 mm to 110 mm diameter: 91.7% of the speed and torque, in return for stability and traction

        System

        • Thermocouple feedback to the temperature controller
        • GPS tracker and Wi-Fi/Bluetooth module
        • LiDAR obstacle detection
        • Mobile or laptop user interface

        Tools: Siemens NX modelling, function structures, requirement lists, thermal and drivetrain calculations

        DataPython

        Mapping temperature onto a deformed mesh

        Research Project, Intelligent Forming Systems, TU Clausthal – IMET. Team of five. Supervisors: Dr. Thierry Fothe and Prof. Dr.-Ing. Johannes Buhl.

        In steel forming tests, temperature and strain come from different cameras with different coordinate frames and time bases. The project transforms the thermal data into the coordinate system of the deformed strain mesh and combines all 24 frames into one interactive viewer.

        Data alignment

        • Temperature was recorded vertically and strain horizontally; the grids were adjusted to match the specimen
        • Values at the fracture point were checked to match
        • Each strain value is assigned its temperature

        Outcome

        • Interactive framework correlating strain and thermal data over time
        • Fixed reference points give consistent mapping
        • Frame navigation and point-based analysis of damage evolution

        Future scope

        • Higher-resolution specimen images
        • Standalone software with file upload
        • Automated sync, alignment and mapping
        • Real-time mapping during live experiments

        Tools: thermal camera and strain data, Python, interactive plotting

        GeometryResearch

        Feature recognition from 3D scans

        Paper "Feature-Based Reverse Engineering in Circular Design", TU Clausthal, 04/2025 – 08/2025. With Raghav Dixit, Sakshi Mohan Gaikwad and Ashwanth Kumar Coimbatore Ramachandran.

        A scanned part is a triangle mesh with no holes, ridges or fillets defined in it. The paper builds a lightweight pipeline that finds those features using curvature analysis and region growing, so a CAD model can be rebuilt from the scan more easily.

        Pipeline

        • Normals from k-nearest neighbors (k = 30)
        • Poisson surface reconstruction, depth 8
        • Laplacian smoothing, 5 iterations
        • PCA curvature and thresholding
        • Region growing with a 50-vertex minimum cluster

        Findings

        • Thresholding separates ridges, fillets and hole rims
        • Size filtering cut 276 clusters to 16 meaningful ones
        • Curvature plus adjacency beats curvature alone

        Limitations noted

        • Fixed thresholds need manual tuning
        • Size filtering may remove minor features
        • Next: adaptive thresholds and edge-preserving filters

        Tools: Python, Open3D, Siemens NX, point clouds and meshes

        ManufacturingCAM

        CAM simulation of a rocket landing tray holder

        Computer Integrated Manufacturing, TU Clausthal, supervised by Prof. Dr. David Inkermann. Report dated 21 June 2025, with Nived Muraleedharan Nambiar.

        The landing tray holder of a self-landing rocket, with an integrated cable duct, was analyzed against DfX principles and redesigned for manufacturability without changing its function. It was then virtually machined in Siemens NX on a 3-axis mill.

        Machining sequence Each block is one operation, sized by machining time.
        StartTotal 00:55:14 (cutting 00:42:33, non-cutting 00:12:41)
        Design changes for manufacturability (6)
        OriginalOptimizedWhy
        Sharp corners10 mm edge blendAvoids stress and handling risks, better appearance
        Thin walls around the cable ductThickened by extruding both sidesHigh stress and deformation risk
        OverhangRemoved and made flatLess complexity, easier machining
        Non-uniform mounting holesAll remodelled to 16 mmOne drilling operation and one tool
        Sharp edges (sketch 13)10 mm edge blendBetter tool access, less machining time
        Sharp edges and joints10 mm edge blendFaster machining, better appearance

        DfX review

        • Manufacturing: flat, parallel surfaces, 2 mm minimum wall
        • Assembly: accessible cable duct, 8 mounting holes
        • Recycling: single material, aluminum

        Guidelines applied

        • Internal joints filleted at 1 mm or more
        • Walls above 2 mm
        • Standardized hole sizes
        • Fewer overhangs and undercuts

        Result

        • Feasible on a 3-axis milling machine
        • Lower complexity, better tool life, simpler assembly
        • 10 operations from roughing to countersinking

        Tools: Siemens NX CAD and CAM, DfX methods
